title: IR Sensor: Reading the Floor
description: Component lesson. No sound this time — light you can't see, bounced off whatever's directly underneath.

content.value: The ultrasonic sensor looks outward, for obstacles ahead. ARIA also needs something that looks straight down, to tell a dark line from the light floor around it — the foundation of line following, which you'll build for real later in this module.

An IR sensor module has an emitter (a small infrared LED, invisible to human eyes) and a detector right next to it. The emitter shines infrared light straight down; the detector watches for it to bounce back. Light surfaces reflect a lot of it back; dark surfaces absorb most of it. The detector's output pin simply reports which one just happened — HIGH or LOW, exactly like Module 4's digital signals.

content.title: ⚫⚪ Slide the surface underneath
content.hint: Drag the slider slowly across a black/white boundary and watch the pin flip the instant the colour changes.

content.value: There's no image here, no camera, nothing rich or detailed — just one bit of information: reflecting a lot, or not. That simplicity is exactly what makes it fast and cheap, and it's plenty for the job it does: a controller reading this pin many times a second can react to a changing floor almost instantly.

Part          IR reflectance sensor module (e.g. TCRT5000)
Output        digital HIGH/LOW (some models also give an analog reading)
Range         a few millimetres to a couple of centimetres above the surface
Price         ≈ ₹20–40 each — ARIA uses two, side by side

Height above the surface matters more than you'd expect: too far and even white stops reflecting enough IR back to register. That's why line-follower sensors are mounted low and close to the floor, not up on the chassis deck.

Key takeaway: an IR sensor shines infrared light down and reads how much bounces back — light surfaces reflect strongly (HIGH), dark surfaces absorb it (LOW). It's a simple digital reading, and that simplicity is the point.

quiz.question: What does an IR reflectance sensor's output pin actually report?
options: An image of the surface below
Whether the emitted infrared light bounced back strongly or was absorbed
The exact colour of the surface
quiz.explain: It's a simple reflectance measurement, not an image — light back (white) versus absorbed (black), reported as HIGH or LOW.

quiz.question: Why are line-follower IR sensors mounted very close to the floor rather than higher up on the chassis?
options: Too much height weakens the reflected IR signal until even white surfaces stop registering reliably
Height has no effect on the reading
quiz.explain: The sensor depends on enough reflected light reaching the detector — distance from the surface directly affects how strong that signal is.

quiz.question: Why is a simple HIGH/LOW reading enough for line following, rather than needing a full image?
options: It isn't enough — real line followers use cameras
The job (dark line vs light floor) only needs one bit of information, so anything richer would be unnecessary complexity
IR sensors can't produce more detail than that, even if it were useful
quiz.explain: Matching the sensor to the job: distinguishing two surface types needs exactly one bit, and a simple digital reading delivers it fast and cheap.
